en: Preface to the *Xianxing Shichaos* (A Manual for Practice: An Abridgment of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* with Supplements) Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Chongyi Monastery in Jingzhao.
The virtue of the precepts is inconceivable, surpassing all other phenomena;
it serves as the guiding track for the five vehicles and is truly the foundation of the three [vehicles].
The precious vessel for crossing over!
Relying upon the teachings to establish and cultivate it, the merits of concentration and wisdom are beyond compare;
in upholding the Buddha-dharma, all various scriptures find their ultimate rest here.
Ever since the Great Master was in the world, he exclusively propagated this scripture;
down to the four reliances, his legacy has remained unaltered.
Reaching the age of the Semblance Dharma, the times have gradually become turbid and corrupt.
They contend for supremacy within the realm of words and debate matters that do not manifest in physical form.
Thus, their teachings were transmitted across the mountain ranges and heard through nine generations;
they stand out as preeminent among their peers, for it is solely through their wisdom and skillful means.
If one wishes to clarify and exalt his conduct and demeanor, to rectify and sustain the Buddhist teachings;
to establish a model for posterity and instruct those of later learning;
and to restore the profound cord that has been severed and re-erect the great banner that has already fallen—then he may be examined and evaluated in detail.
Is it not that relying on the void is easy when it comes to form and sound, whereas following the tracks of actual affairs is difficult to accomplish, requiring one to be as pure as dew?
Thus, the former masters relied upon the Vinaya-piṭaka; they pointed to the facts, examined the texts, and put them into practice.
Thus, while the written record is faithful to the facts, the circumstances upon which it relies are indeed numerous and excessive.
Furthermore, my learning is neither refined nor extensive, and my speculative assertions are particularly many;
my selection of analogies lacks thorough discussion, and various heterodox views have thus accumulated.
This has led to the analysis of transgressions and contradictions, where the degrees of gravity differ by multiples;
the maintenance of various systems, where similarities and differences are distinguished.

Were it not for one who comprehends the rise and fall of the underlying intent of the teachings and examines the truth or falsity of various doctrines, who could resolve profound doubts, dispel accumulated entanglements, synthesize the tenets of the schools, and elucidate the characteristics of mental formations?

I have always regretted that among the records left behind by the masters of previous generations, they merely consist of commentaries on the treatises concerning the establishment or rejection of doctrines and essential excerpts of dialogues;
as for those that manifest practical worldly affairs and provide a model for future learners, there is not a single such work to be found among them.
At that time, there were those whose intentions were sharp and whose actions were practiced, yet the literary expression remained confined within the *Yìjí* (Collection on Meaning);
or again, there were those who listed many flowery phrases, yet their engagement with the capacities of sentient beings was insufficient;
or there were those who merely titled their works "Karmavācanā," failing to proclaim the characteristics of its fulfillment.
If one relies solely on the literal text, one will fail to discern the preceding matters;
furthermore, the phrasing is fragmented and disordered, making it difficult to examine and verify.
Thus, those who seek [the truth] do so not because they lack accumulated learning, but because [the text] is thus.
As for those who seek to comprehend [this], none can fully master it without refined cultivation.
During my leisure from listening and collecting [teachings], I have glanced through various texts;
though they do not all align with my own intent, each possesses its own strengths and weaknesses.
With a brilliant resolve, he set forth his mission, unhesitatingly unfolding his pen to record everything.

He encompassed the authentic texts of diverse schools and summarized the various expositions found throughout the scriptures; he further investigated the records left by the sages and saints of the Western Regions as well as the literary chronicles of the virtuous predecessors of this land.
He searched out and scrutinized all points of agreement and difference, exhausting every detail through rigorous examination.
That which is long-established and essential shall certainly be recorded, so as to assist broad knowledge;
that which is excessive or spurious shall certainly be excised, so as to perfect the comprehensive meaning.
Sometimes elaborate phrasing is used to clarify practical applications, and sometimes concise indications are employed to group related items together.
In some cases, the text is interrupted but connected by its meaning; in others, the inquiry is posed through provisional questions.
Thus, from beginning to end, they illuminate one another, with the hidden and the manifest appearing in alternation.

Furthermore, the *Karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) currently in practice, the right and wrong of various administrative affairs, the correct protocols for guiding the laity, and miscellaneous rules for those who have left the household life—all of these are gathered together as a single perspective of this school, intended to save the new students from laborious effort!
Yet, when their views accord with my own, I strike at their major points; when they hold divergent doctrines, I reject their prolixity. Who would delight in such prolixity?
It is simply because there was no other recourse!
Why is this? If one were to briefly abridge and extract only the general outline, there would always be a deficiency for practical application;
yet if one were to arbitrarily include non-urgent remarks, they would become an object of avoidance in the compilation.
Now, having planned and measured this work with a view to moderation, I have endeavored to be concise;
it is intended as a remedy for emergencies and a preparation for sudden needs, compiled into three fascicles.

If my thoughts are insufficient regarding current events, such that there are indeed omissions in the explanations of practice, I have merely indicated the essential purports here so as to broaden the understanding of future generations.
However, the text of this single treatise unfolds its meaning across three sections.
The first volume encompasses various affairs and establishes the protocols for their practical application;
the middle volume follows the essence of the precepts, establishing the procedures for observance, violation, and repentance.
The lower fascicle consists of essential practices according to individual capacity, arising from reliance on specific events;
these are all detailed as presented in the text, and one may assume there is no confusion therein.
However, because the objects and circumstances are truly numerous, it is indeed difficult to categorize them systematically.
Now, in selecting these categories according to their mutual affinities, I have used headings to mark the titles;

yet, as for comprehensively grasping the great framework, I fear that the detailed branches and currents may not yet be fully understood, so I shall further summarize them by way of ten topical sections, so that they may serve as a mirror to clarify distant meanings.

The Great Outline of the Sangha’s Net Chapter Seven: The Causes and Conditions for Receiving Precepts Chapter Eight: [Title missing] (The Collection of Conditions for Receiving Precepts)

The Section on the Names and Rewards of the Offenses against the Precepts. Chapter Fourteen: The Section on Explaining the Characteristics of the Individual Precepts.

The Method for Constructing Images and Temples; Chapter Twenty-three: Rules for Inviting and Providing for [Guests]; Chapter Twenty-four: Methods for Guiding the Laity;

Chapter Twenty-six: Miscellaneous Essential Practices; Chapter Twenty-seven: The World-transcending Right Action; Chapter Twenty-eight:
The Specific Rules for Bhikṣus and Śrāmaṇeras Based on the Dharma; Chapter Twenty-nine: The Specific Conduct of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha; Chapter Thirty:
The Specific Conduct of Various Schools. Part One: Preface on the Intent of the Arising of the Teaching.
When the Perfect Man arises in the world, he benefits all things through established methods;
he establishes teachings according to circumstances, for there is no principle that is bestowed in vain.
As the Treatise says:
Relying upon the gate of great compassion, the Vinaya is taught.
Thus, the Vinaya states:
"The World-Honored One, out of compassionate concern, expounds the Dharma for them."

Second, it was established so that the Buddha’s Dharma would not be treated as inferior by non-Buddhists (tīrthika), thereby manifesting the supremacy of the Buddha-Dharma and the loftiness of its path; thus this precept was formulated.
Observe the Vinaya below: all those things which were prescribed were intended for those who harbored heterodox arts.
Therefore, the text says:
"If one does not compile and conclude [the teachings], it will allow non-Buddhists (tīrthika) to produce further [erroneous] arguments.
Third, [this section] comes as a response to divergent schools."
The schools, however, possess many distinctions:
for instance, in the Sarvāstivāda school, the precept texts are both elaborate and abbreviated; their indication of the essential substance is not yet complete;
they fix the duration of time according to worldly conventions, yet their application of the Dharma lacks a universal standard.
Now, in the Dharmaguptaka school, both persons and the Dharma follow an orderly sequence, and its regulations and applications are manifold;
its guidance exists solely to foster wholesome roots, and the intent of its established teachings lies in being manifest yet concise.
Above, we have clarified that the teachings arise; now, we shall examine this based on our own school.
For the teachings do not emerge in isolation but must depend upon persons;
since persons differ, the teachings are likewise not uniform.
Therefore, its capacity to gather, guide, and provide vast salvation is truly manifold.
What is valued lies in grasping its fundamental exposition; indeed, it is difficult to scrutinize its detailed ramifications.
Thus, the principles of restriction and expansion are established, and the verification of their intent lies in benefiting humanity.
To clarify the observance and violation [of the precepts], it is understood that the underlying intent lies in remaining free from transgression.
Now, if the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is condensed and divided according to five categories, the purpose for which the teaching was established becomes evident!

First, regarding the distinction between prohibitive and essential precepts: essential evil applies to both the *vaipulya* (transformative) and *vinaya* (disciplinary) codes, whereas prohibitive precepts arise specifically due to transgressions.
Thus, while the wording of essential precepts is relaxed, their meaning is urgent; that is to say, following each of the grave precepts, there are corresponding provisions for exceptions (*anujñā*).
Although the wording provides for exceptions, these exceptions actually result in the commission of an offense.
Even if one were to achieve observance, it would be truly difficult to maintain.
For instance, in the case of lust, there is no pleasure throughout the three periods [of time]; whereas in the case of disparagement, one must practice compassion and rescue from beginning to end.
Since these are fundamental forms of greed and hatred, how can one restrain the mind so that it does not stray?
Thus we know that the principle lies in urgent protection!
Prohibitions are initially established to restrain; if they prove beneficial, exceptions are granted;
when the abuse of these exceptions arises, prohibitions are once again reinstated.
Is this not because, in order to preserve the transformation of the world, one fears falling into the pit of error?

The Great Compassionate One established his teachings with the sole intent of rectifying such failings; thus, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* fully establishes two modes—the lenient and the urgent—so that by following them, one may achieve universal understanding!
Second, regarding the opening of prohibitions and the subsequent re-imposition of them, the teaching thus applies to both time periods.
Therefore, the following passage states:

"Because the World-Honored One is one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom, he may lift a prohibition after it has been established, or re-establish a prohibition after it has been lifted; this refers to the teaching for future generations."
As stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:
"Even though it is that which I have prescribed, if it is not considered pure in other regions, then one should not employ it;
even though it is not that which I have prescribed, if it must be practiced in other regions, one must practice it."
This is the teaching of the Tathāgata while in the world!
Nevertheless, these two teachings are mutually integrated, each encompassing the other.
Thirdly, because the karmic retribution one receives varies in strength, the teachings are likewise applied with varying degrees of emphasis.
In terms of the established precepts, there is profound prevention and demarcation; in terms of practice, the mountain-dwelling and worldly traditions differ.
Fourth, awakening through individual capacity is prioritized.
Is it not the case that the teachings are separated by their relative gravity and that the five schools hold differing attachments?
Fifth, regarding the relative nature of ritual matters (*śīla*) and the Dharma:
the Dharma consists solely of formal models; if one deviates from its essential intent, the ritual matter will not be accomplished.
Ritual matters, however, pertain to human sentiments and dispositions; therefore, their success or failure is determined according to the specific circumstances of each situation.
Sometimes they rely on the conditions of the three natures, and sometimes they arise in response to worldly censure.
For now, I shall briefly cite several instances so that you may have a slight understanding of their approach.
As for the comprehensive summaries and overarching principles, they all aim at rescuing and guiding the common masses, establishing the teachings out of a heart that embraces the mundane world.
Therefore, the text says:
"For what reason did the World-Honored One establish the training in increased morality?
It was for the sake of subduing the three poisons!"
What is meant by "learning"?
It is for the sake of seeking the four fruits!
The intent behind the regulations described in the subsequent sections merely follows upon the preceding matters, so that those who come later may trace the branches back to their root.
Second is the intention regarding the gravity of the established precepts.
The two intentions of lightness and gravity are truly difficult to adjudicate. Why is this?
If one traces back the teachings that were able to be bestowed, the Teacher was a person who had exhausted all capacities for discernment;
Furthermore, if we examine the person for whom this was done, that individual was merely a vessel for the medicine;
thus, the medicine and the ailment struck one another, yielding benefits beyond measure.
How could this be judged by mere sentiment? It is certainly not something that can be fathomed through words or debate!
Although its distant origins have been re-examined, its actual influence extends to future generations.
This is evident from the text itself; what need is there for further corroboration?
Now, I shall provide a brief introduction to this work, which consists of seven parts:
First, the gradual and sudden arising of revulsion;
second, the classification of the definitive karma;
third, the differences in the retributive fruits.
Fourth, the superiority and inferiority of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*);
fifth, the reality or unreality of arising emotions;
sixth, the mutual establishment of permissions and prohibitions.
Seventh, they differ according to their practice, such as the two modes of "righteousness" (yi) and "tranquility" (jing)!
All such examples are the fundamental intention of the established teachings and the essential substance of their definitive judgments.
Regarding the third pair, the intent of the judgment concerning the teachings based on the facts:

since the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward, nearly six hundred years have passed; various masters have engaged in speculative excavation, dividing and judging right from wrong, vying with one another to seal their own positions as either identical or different, beyond all reckoning.
This is truly because those who investigate do not recognize the fundamental tenet, while those who practice are muddled regarding the original purpose.
Therefore, one who studies must certainly rely on the scriptures as the ultimate standard, and one who upholds the teaching must certainly wear the true texts upon themselves.
Why should one be subjected to such censure and disparagement, or even sink into such contemptuous reproach?
Now, in adjudicating what constitutes an offense or its non-occurrence, we must return to the basis of the vows received;
since the vows were received according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, how can one claim that the subsequent application of the precepts may follow a different school?
Fearing that you may still not understand the general outline, I shall further demonstrate its specific boundaries:
to rashly use what one has personally studied to judge the transgressions or observances of others—
if one should thereby incur faults and failings, it can only be due to the ignorance of not having studied.
Now, a universal standard has been established to serve as a common benchmark; with a single glance at these articles and precepts, one attains a vast and clear understanding.
Fourth, regarding the application of the textual meanings of the various sections:

the Vinaya-piṭaka as a whole is fundamentally a single text, yet because the capacities and realizations of sentient beings differ, it has resulted in various interpretations standing as high as mountains.

Therefore, according to their respective inclinations and desires, they established their own schools, vying with one another to adopt the writings of the great assemblies to compile the canons of their own traditions.
Consequently, there arose differences in emphasis between the light and the grave, divergent paths regarding what constitutes an offense and its maintenance;
the presence and absence of precepts alternated, while periods of decline and flourishing appeared in turn.
Now, we establish the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* as the primary authority;
however, when performing ritual procedures, if it is necessary to employ other schools' texts, they must not be disregarded.
Thus, the *Sammohavinodanī* states:
The Vinaya consists of four parts; those of great virtue who possess supernormal powers should extract them and cause others to know them.
The first part refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
Second, following the original;

third, the words of the Dharma Master: this refers to the Buddha first preaching the original [text], which was then extensively analyzed and propagated by five hundred arhats—namely, the author of the treatise.
The four applications of the mind refer to the application of skillful means through the mind, as well as the extensive explanations found in the Tripiṭaka and other texts.
First, one contemplates the fundamental; next, one attends to the meaning of the phrases; finally, one observes the words of the Dharma teacher.
One should adopt those [teachings] that accord with the text and phrases, but not take up those that do not. The sixth fascicle explains the methods of the Vinaya masters in detail.
The main text is thus.
However, the affairs of action and withdrawal are truly difficult, and the principles of acceptance and rejection are not easy;
therefore, I shall briefly recount their great exegesis to serve as a guide for those free from delusion.

This means that within this school, both the text and its meaning are complete; regarding the practical applications (*vastu*), there is no deficiency, such that the school is self-sufficient and what need is there to seek elsewhere?

As for other schools, where Vinaya texts are incomplete, their practices have already been superseded by those previously established; where there is meaning but no text, or no text but the practice exists, [the former is resolved through interpretation and the latter is adopted].
All such examples have been drawn from external schools to complete this treatise.
Furthermore, regarding the categories cited, those whose meanings and implications are closely related may be used for corroboration;
however, those that differ in their urgency, gravity, or the distinctions between right and wrong must not be adopted, even if they conform to the original treatises.
Therefore, the text lists four explanations to allow for an examination of their merits and defects.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) uses the analogy of a seal on ink; its meaning is likewise the same.
If one clarifies it in this manner, then the mind and its objects will reflect one another, and every movement will accord with the established principles.
Whether one adopts the elaborate, the concise, or the intermediate versions, how could the underlying principle remain obscured?

If one does not reflect upon and examine the various sections of the canon, but instead adheres dogmatically to a single corner of it, then when engaging with specific matters, one’s understanding will be incomplete; and when collating the texts, there will be no basis for verification.

Consequently, people follow their own subjective opinions and vie with one another over right and wrong, mutually accusing each other of being deluded. This is truly due to a lack of authoritative teaching.

If the textual provisions of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* were limited, then those matters could not be universally applied; one would instead have to resort to the texts of other schools to accomplish the requirements of those other schools.

If, within two Vinayas, both the text and the meaning are clearly elucidated such that there is no basis for selection or rejection, then both emerge as the True Dharma and may be adopted according to one's inclination.
However, when practicing the authentic teachings, one should personally examine them, fearing that what has been transmitted through hearsay might corrupt the truth.
Furthermore, there are briefly six ways of upholding the Vinaya in the world.

First, there are those who uphold only a single section, such as the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and do not employ the doctrines of other schools—such as the examples regarding the wearing of robes or the administration of medicine—even when the text lacks them; they merely hold to their own manual.

Second, there are omissions in the relevant sections of our own school’s texts, which necessitate drawing upon external citations, such as those concerning the maintenance of robes and the addition of medicinal substances found in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Third, within our own tradition, there are doctrinal interpretations where the textual passages are not explicit, such as those regarding insanity, the fulfillment of quorum, and sleep or deafness.

4. The textual meaning of this section is fully elucidated, yet it is discarded by other schools, such as the practice of abandoning the pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) or the direct recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

5. It concurrently adopts the five collections (*pañcapiṭaka*), universally harmonizing them with the Vinaya school, as seen in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, for instance, in the account of not testing non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) until they have cooled down.

The sixth concerns the ultimate destination: the Mahāyāna’s supreme pinnacle, as seen in the *Laṅkāvatāra* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, which includes such practices as keeping monastic quarters free of smoke, prohibiting alcohol, meat, and the five pungent herbs, and refraining from the eight kinds of impure wealth.
These six masters each uphold correct teachings, none of which deviate from the intent of the Sages;
however, due to their two perspectives—comprehensive and limited—their applications and interpretations differ.
The principles followed in this *Chao* (Excerpts) intend to adopt the views of the third and sixth masters.
The rest should also be consulted as appropriate; gains and losses depend on the occasion, for one must know the proper time!
This is the fifth point: the intent of resolving and clarifying the text and its meaning.
Now, the principle is fundamentally beyond names, yet names are established to mark its ultimate tenet.
Names manifest according to their referents; thus, this text is prepared in response to those referents.

Yet, upon examining this Vinaya-piṭaka, one finds that both its words and its matters are comprehensive. However, because the intervening ages are vast and distant, the traces of its former splendor have faded;
as time has shifted, many matters within the Dharma have become incomplete or lost.
Furthermore, the five masters who collected these teachings held differing views;
subsequently, due to errors in translation that missed the original intent, arbitrary constructions were fabricated;
and finally, through scribal errors and omissions, these inaccuracies were perpetuated through successive transmission.
Therefore, in pursuing these investigations, my perplexities have been many.
Now, I shall synthesize them to clarify the overarching vision.
If both the text and its meaning are deficient, one may cite a single instance to serve as an analogy for all others.
In some cases, although [the text] exists according to principle, it fails to establish the preceding matter;
in other cases, although it is complete in its wording, it is deficient in meaning, and thus one must determine it by means of the meaning.
Therefore, the treatise states that "principle is what is authoritative."

Alternatively, although a certain interpretation may necessarily be established, if there is no textual authority within one's own school, one must synthesize the views of various schools to quell further criticism.
However, when the meaning of the text is definitively settled, it is truly difficult to either reject or establish an alternative;
this is possible only for those who deeply clarify the characteristics of the Vinaya and are proficient in understanding its permissions and prohibitions.
Otherwise, one will burden one’s own mind and certainly derive no benefit for the external object. Thus, the Vinaya states: "The text and meaning are both identical;

the text is identical but the meaning differs; the text differs but the meaning is identical; the text and meaning are both different. These four cases have been fully set forth regarding advancing and retreating; there is no need for further elaboration or explanation.
However, one who seeks to definitively judge right from wrong must thoroughly comprehend the essential principles of the Vinaya-piṭaka and recognize the textual nuances that follow the Sūtras;
only by understanding what has been elucidated by the six masters mentioned above can one fully investigate the traces of this teaching.
Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"A bhikṣu definitively knows the characteristics of the Vinaya through three matters:
first, the origin; second, the formal enactment of the precept; and third, the subsequent application."

One should contemplate and examine the two divisions of the Vinaya, as well as the Abhidharma, the Vinaya itself, and the Ekottarika Āgama, regarding what is permitted or prohibited, and what is light or heavy.
For example, the five primary colors are impure and thus prohibited;
that which is not color is pure and thus not prohibited.
In this manner, one has already employed the weighing of the beginning and the end!
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*) also states:
"A bhikṣu who can know the five characteristics is said to understand the Vinaya and does not look to the faces of others."
The text is abbreviated as above; for a detailed account, one should refer to what is explained therein.
Regarding the sixth point, the meaning of what is expounded by the teaching:
although the textual passages that expound this teaching are vast and extensive, if one summarizes their essential purport, they clarify nothing more than upholding and violating the precepts.
However, regarding the objects of observance and transgression, these objects encompass both the internal and the external;
the internal refers to the karmic entanglements of the active mind, while the external refers to the conformity or opposition of circumstantial events.
Provided that one allows the teachings and practice to follow one another so that there is no transgression from beginning to end, this constitutes observance.

If one has been born without learning and has heard nothing of the Dharma, yet performs good or evil deeds—wherein the principle encompasses both merit and retribution—and one now wishes to adjudicate an offense, it is sufficient that the act correspond to the teaching;
one does not inquire into the truth or falsity of the circumstances, as all such cases are termed "transgressions."
This is what is generally termed "upholding and violating" the precepts!

Regarding the formal offenses established in this treatise, when investigating all forms of disciplinary punishment, one must invariably constrain the preliminary expedients so as to bring about the resulting karmic fruit;
furthermore, the assessment must be based on a rigorous examination of the actual circumstances, ensuring that the gravity of the offense accords with both principle and the teachings.
Thus, the distinctions are clear and decisive; how could there be any further confusion or redundancy?
This is what is meant by the separate categories of "upholding" and "violating.
Seventh is the intention regarding the universal and specific applications of the teachings established for the seven groups of monastics and laity.
The teachings that manifest the principles have many paths and can be sought through human sentiment; they are broadly divided into two categories.
The first is called the "teachings of transformation" (*huàjiào*).
These apply universally to both monastics and the laity.
It merely provides a general clarification of cause and effect and an understanding of the heterodox and the orthodox;
it categorizes karmic practices, which are profound and difficult to discern,
and reveals the retributions that follow, which are clear and easy to describe.
The second refers to the teaching on practice,
which applies exclusively to the internal community.
It determines what is to be adopted or rejected, establishes the framework and its details, clarifies observance and transgression, and resolves doubts and obstructions.
When pointing directly to phenomena to explain them thoroughly, the text allows for no redundancy;
yet when defining offenses and making clear judgments, there is the fault of double-counting the matter.
Thus, as these two teachings circulate in turn, they are not without points of overlap.
If one judges by taking the entire school as a whole, the principle becomes self-evident.
If it is said that the internal mind’s compliance or resistance takes the Principle as its primary focus, then this accords with the Teaching of Transformation;
if external conduct and actions necessarily involve guarding body and speech, then this relies upon the Teaching of Practice.
However, those who violate the teachings of transformation (the *śāsana*) receive only the retribution for the path of karma;
those who contravene the teachings of practice (the *ācāra*) incur the additional gravity of offenses against the holy regulations (*ārya-vinaya*).
Thus, the Sūtra says:
The offense is grave for one who has received the precepts, while it is light for one who has not; this is self-evident from the extensive text.

The reason for further differentiating them is the fear that [practitioners] might become confused regarding the fundamental essence of the two teachings and thus recklessly discourse on the right and wrong of karmic conduct;
therefore, a single gate is established to permanently serve as a means of clear distinction.
Eighth, the meaning of the commonalities and differences in the ritual procedures for the two communities of monks and nuns.
Since the two communities share the same precepts and regulations, their formal procedures and legal principles are identical;
as for the practical application of rituals, they are modeled upon the monastic rules.
These are fully contained within the various sections; they should be applied in detail according to the specific circumstances.
As for distinguishing the characteristics of an offense, these are already present in the *Prātimokṣa* itself.
Those points that are concealed and difficult to discern are fully detailed in the *Anuvyañjana*.

There are further precepts categorized by stage, meaning that their gravity differs, their presence or absence varies, and while the transgressions may be identical, the conditions for them differ; these are those practices prevalent in the present age whose specific characteristics are difficult to discern.
Furthermore, the rules for individual conduct and communal conduct will be set forth subsequently within the section on the specific rules for nuns.
This merely distinguishes their categories; it has not yet revealed the specific meanings of their origins.
The various points of divergence are fully detailed in the Great Commentary (*Daishu*). Section Nine, Part Two:
The Agreement and Differences Regarding the Conduct of the Three Lower Assemblies.
Regarding the two groups of śrāmaṇeras, if one considers their precept-substance (śīla-tattva), it is identical to that of the great bhikṣus in its unmanifest nature (avijñapti);
yet when examining their original number, only ten are explicitly revealed;
as for the remaining practices they follow, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The offenses are categorized in the fifth section, situated at the end of all the precepts.
As for those external practices that differ and involve distinct criteria for adoption or rejection, each is explained in detail within its own respective section.
For a śikṣamāṇā, the six dharmas constitute the core of her training; the substance of the precepts does not arise again.

First, the citation of the authentic scriptures is clarified; second, the spurious teachings prevalent in the world are clarified; and third, the original intent for composing the *Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) is clarified.

Regarding the first point on the "authentic texts": the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is the fundamental division (*mūla-nikāya*); the others are the five divisions, including the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), which is the school followed by the author of the *Chao*; the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya); the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya); and the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya* (Liberation Vinaya). These possess their respective *prātimokṣa* matrices (*mātṛkā*). The *Vātsīputrīya-vinaya* has not yet arrived; this is distinguished according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.

The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, the *Sudarsana-śāstra*, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* were transmitted together; the *Vinaya-sūtra* and the *Vibhāṣā-prabhāvṛtti* explain the Saṃmitīya school, along with the commentary by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha;

Now, as for those who dwell within the ocean of the Buddha and partake of the flavor of the Dharma stream, whose physical forms are ranked among the monastic community, their practice consists of only three stages.

If one reveres and upholds the right precepts and possesses thorough knowledge of their observance and transgression, then the essential substance and characteristics are complete within the middle fascicle.
Once one's own practice is perfected and external virtues manifest their function, then the governing principles are preserved within the upper fascicle.
The various ways in which the virtues of self and others are accomplished are extensively detailed within the lower fascicles, where their specific features are clearly revealed.
These three [fascicles] encompass all practices, such that no practice is left uncollected;
these three fascicles subsume all texts, such that no text is not treated with thoroughness.
Thus, when matters and categories coincide, it is even more difficult to measure and compare them;
yet if they were to be dispersed and explained over a long course, there would be little room for discussion.
If one must instead divide them according to their specific characteristics, the fault lies in excessive fragmentation.
Now, following what is appropriate, I shall provide a brief summary to clarify the ultimate aim;
thus, by grasping the handle and lifting the net, the individual hairs and meshes will naturally fall into order.
As you unfold and examine this, let it serve as a guide for each specific matter and each particular circumstance.
